findings.evidence: "Check the message again and enter all six."
findings.fix: Name the actual channel, e.g. "Check the text message we sent and enter all six digits."
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - first message entry ("5 digits" message)
findings.violation: "The message" doesn't specify which delivery channel the code was sent through (SMS, email, app), leaving the instruction ambiguous about where to look.

findings.fix: Propose a preventive fix such as an input mask/live digit counter that blocks entry past 6 digits, or justify why none is needed.
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - first message entry, "Predictable mistake" / "Suggested fix" fields
findings.violation: Flagging a mistake as predictable implies it recurs often enough to warrant prevention, yet no mitigation (e.g., restricting the field to 6 digits) is proposed.

findings.evidence: "This verification code expired 10 minutes after it was sent, which stops an intercepted code from being reused later."
findings.fix: Cut the rationale clause and lead with the action: "This code has expired. Request a new one and enter it here."
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - second message entry (expired code)
findings.violation: The message justifies the security policy to the user instead of focusing on the needed action, adding irrelevant, oddly technical content to an inline error.

findings.evidence: "selectable, offers a resend code button in place of the message"
findings.fix: Rewrite as a plain sentence, e.g. "Replace the message with a 'Resend code' button."
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - second message entry, "Suggested fix" field
findings.violation: The fix description is a garbled fragment inconsistent with the terse one-word format used in every other entry, making its meaning and scope unclear.

findings.fix: Clear the field (or mark it visibly stale) when the expiry error fires, rather than preserving it as-is.
findings.location: Two-factor setup, verification code - second message entry, "Input on resubmission" field
findings.violation: Preserving the expired code's digits gives no visual indication the value must change, inviting the user to resubmit the same invalid code unchanged.

findings.fix: Include the year, e.g. "This promo code ended on 30 June 2026."
findings.location: Billing, promo code - first message entry (expired promo)
findings.violation: The date omits the year, making the expiration ambiguous for a user revisiting the flow near a year boundary.

findings.fix: Apply a consistent definition of "predictable mistake" across both promo-code messages, or state the reasoning that distinguishes them.
findings.location: Billing, promo code - first message entry, "Predictable mistake" field
findings.violation: Entering a stale/expired promo code (often shared long after it lapses) is at least as foreseeable as the plan-mismatch case below, which is marked "yes" - the criterion is applied inconsistently between the two promo-code entries.

findings.fix: Suggest a preventive fix, such as disabling or graying out the promo field when the selected plan is ineligible for the entered code.
findings.location: Billing, promo code - second message entry (plan mismatch), "Predictable mistake" / "Suggested fix" fields
findings.violation: As with the digit-count message, a mistake flagged as predictable has no proposed prevention, even though the conflict (code requires annual, plan is monthly) is knowable before submission.

findings.evidence: "Change the plan to annual, or remove the code."
findings.fix: Add a secondary cue (highlight or link) on the plan selector so the user can locate the field the message refers to.
findings.location: Billing, promo code - second message entry, message text
findings.violation: The instructed fix lives in the plan selector, a different field from the one displaying the message, but only the promo code field carries the error signal - nothing flags the plan selector itself.

findings.evidence: "Signal: bold text set larger than the field label, icon" (identical in all four entries)
findings.fix: Vary signal weight/icon type by severity, reserving the heaviest treatment for blocking errors and a lighter one for optional or informational notices.
findings.violation: The same high-intensity visual treatment is used for messages of very different severity (an optional "continue without one" notice vs. a blocking expired-code error), flattening the hierarchy and making urgency hard to triage at a glance.
